data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["In engineering/medicine, we often implicitly trust laws of physics/biology to hold (induction), whereas Popper explicitly forbids this trust.","Surviving a test in science is not equivalent to lacking a defect; a theory can be unfalsified yet completely wrong in ways not yet tested."],"overturn_conditions":["If it is shown that avoiding known errors necessarily implies an expectation that unknown errors are less likely (hidden induction).","If the context requires positive assurance of success (e.g., life-critical systems) where mere 'non-falsification' is insufficient for action."],"shared_structure":["Decision made under total uncertainty of future performance.","Differentiation based solely on known negative attributes (defects/allergies/falsifications).","Preference for the option with the fewest/severe known negatives, without assuming it will succeed."],"source_memory_refs":["bridge_collapse_known_defects","medical_triage_known_allergies"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a surgeon avoids a patient with a known allergy even if other drugs might also fail, a scientist avoids a falsified theory even if corroborated ones might also fail.","Rationality in both cases is defined negatively: avoiding the known disaster, not guaranteeing the cure."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible without smuggling in induction if re-framed as a 'critical risk-management' strategy rather than a probabilistic prediction; however, this defense survives only by accepting the cost that rational action becomes purely negative (avoiding known falsehoods) and cannot positively justify expectations of future success, leaving the agent with no basis to believe the chosen theory will work, only that it has not yet been proven to fail.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent must assign any non-zero subjective probability of success to act rationally, the distinction collapses into pragmatic induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'risk minimization' implicitly assumes that past falsification conditions are relevant to future contexts, it smuggles in an inductive premise about the stability of nature.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the goal of action is positive achievement (success) rather than merely avoiding known failure, the negative justification of corroboration is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Reconstruct the preference as a decision rule under ignorance: since all theories are equally unproven regarding the future (induction is invalid), the only differentiating factor is the set of known errors. Choosing the theory with fewer or less severe known errors (better corroboration) minimizes the risk of acting on a known falsehood. This relies on the logical asymmetry between verification and falsification, not on the assumption that the future resembles the past.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
